chapter_theme: The joy of the quarrel, and the end of the Kural. Sulking is here set above heaven, and above union itself as digestion is above eating; the loser wins, and a man prays for the night to last. The whole work ends not on virtue or God but on a condition about an embrace.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1321-1324 to the woman and 1325-1330 to the man, each explaining their delight. Manakkudavar's commentary ends the entire Kural at 1323 and marks the book's completion there, and calls the group at 1324 the man's eight, so his order of these last verses differs.

1321.reading: The woman says that even though he has no fault, the way he shows his grace has the power to bring on a sulk.

positions.position: It is jealousy: his love is so delightful that others surely enjoy it too, and she can't stand the thought.
positions.quote: யான் எய்தற் பாலதாய இத்தலையளி ஒழிந்தாரும் எய்துவர் எனக்கருதி, அது பொறாமையான் ஊடல்நிகழா நின்றது

positions.position: He reverses the direction: the quarrel, between faultless lovers, builds up their love.

1322.reading: The woman says that even if his fine grace droops a little through the small misery sulking brings, it rises to greatness.
1322.nuance: She is justifying the risk to a friend who has pointed out she could have his kindness without quarrelling. வாடினும், 'though it droop', uses a word for a plant that comes back stronger. Parimelazhagar keeps the concession small: a quarrel with no real fault passes quickly.

1323.reading: The woman asks if there is any heaven to compare with sulking with one to whom one is joined as water to earth.
1323.nuance: Readers of Tamil poetry will recall Kuruntokai 40 here, with its rain and red earth. I offer that as an echo. In the sequence Manakkudavar's text gives, these are the last words of the Kural.

positions.position: Water takes on the character of the ground it's in, so men take on the nature of the women they touch, which is the reason for her sulking. It's a surprisingly suspicious reading of a famous image.
positions.quote: நீர் தான் நின்ற நிலத்தியல்பிற்றாமாறு போலக் காதலரும் தாம் கூடிய மகளிரியல்பினராகலான்

positions.position: Earth and water together combine heat and coolness, and in the same way lovers experience joy and pain as one.
positions.quote: நிலத்தொடு நீரியை தலால் அவை வெப்பமுந்தட்பமுங் கூடியிருக்குமாறு போல்

positions.position: புத்தேள்நாடு isn't a divine world but a new one, which removes heaven from the verse.

1324.reading: Within the sulk that follows an embrace and won't let go arises the weapon that breaks 'my' heart; the speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the man for Manakkudavar.
1324.nuance: Both identify the weapon: his bows and soft words for Parimelazhagar, and soft words (பணிமொழி) for Manakkudavar. Being broken is exactly what she is after, so the battle imagery here is pure pleasure. Compare the same weapon in 1258.

positions.position: The woman answers the friend's question about what will end this sulk.
He calls the group at this point the man's speech.

1325.reading: The man, delighted after making up, says that though men may be faultless, being kept from the soft arms of those they love has a certain something.
1325.nuance: ஆங்கொன்று, 'a certain something', is an honest refusal to name it, and Parimelazhagar takes it that way: the pleasure is beyond words. Even the wrongly accused gets something from this. It matches 1321, in which she sulks at a man with no fault.

1326.reading: The man says digesting what you have eaten is sweeter than eating, and for love sulking is sweeter than union.
1326.nuance: Earthy and unusual, as digestion rarely comes into love poetry. The thought behind it is appetite: as Parimelazhagar says, hunger makes food better, and distance makes union better.

1327.reading: The man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses wins, as can be seen when they come together.
1327.nuance: A paradox with a precise explanation in Parimelazhagar: the one who gives way first gets the great joy, and only later learns this. He adds the first-person point: I gave way, and so I got this joy.

1328.reading: The man asks whether by sulking they might again win that savour which appeared in union, with her forehead wet with sweat.
1328.nuance: உப்பு, 'salt', stands for sweetness here, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as இனிமை, which he explains as all five senses at once, recalling 1101. It's a frankly physical detail near the end of the Kural, and Manakkudavar notes that sulking belongs to both of them.

1329.reading: The man wishes that the bright-jewelled woman would keep on sulking, and that the night would last, so that he may go on pleading.
1329.nuance: The pleading has become what he wants, and not merely a way to get to what he wants. யாமிரப்ப, 'that we may plead': the man who began the book with his might broken now prays for the chance to beg.

1330.reading: The man says sulking is love's pleasure, and the pleasure of sulking is being able to come together and embrace.
1330.nuance: In the received order, the last verse of the entire work ends on பெறின், 'if one gets to'. So 1,330 verses on virtue, wealth and love close with a chained definition and an open condition. Parimelazhagar explains the condition: knowing how far to go is the hard part, so that the union will still be possible.

links.note: 1103 asks whether the Lotus-eyed one's world is sweeter than sleeping on the arms of one's beloved. 1323 repeats the challenge to heaven with a stranger choice: it's the quarrel that outdoes heaven now. Between these two verses, love has come to value its own frictions most.

In 1088, a warrior laments his strength being broken by her forehead, and takes it as defeat. In 1327, the man has worked out that losing is the way to win. The book's military imagery, which begins with injury, ends in a pleasantly ruined scoreboard.

In 1169, the woman in separation says the long nights are crueller than the cruel man himself. In 1329, the man in reunion prays for night to lengthen. The same long night is torment or wish, depending on whether the other person is there.

942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats only after the last meal has digested. 1326 takes the same physician's advice and makes it a rule of love: the pause between meals is what keeps appetite and health.

Both say soft words are the weapon that breaks her defences. In 1258 she says it with bitterness and calls him a thief, and in 1324 she says it with something like eagerness. The weapon hasn't changed, and what she wants from it has.

source_issues: 1323: Manakkudavar's entry ends with கற்பியல் முற்றிற்று ... திருக்குறள் மூலமும் உரையும் முற்றுப்பெற்றன, which marks this verse as the last of the work in his order, unlike the 1330 of the received order. The closing verse of the Kural therefore differs across traditions.
1324: Manakkudavar's note இவையெட்டும் தலைமகன் கூற்று, 'these eight are the man's', doesn't fit its position here and depends on his different order.
1322: Manakkudavar's entry has உடலிற் where ஊடலிற் is required.
1328: Parimelazhagar's gloss has சொல்லோ for கொல்லோ, and his note has the feminine என்றாள் for a verse whose gloss has a male speaker (இவள் நுதல்).
